passage: By the third night after the funeral, Tanvir had answered every relative's call, sorted the bank papers into a blue folder and reminded his mother to eat twice. Damini, nineteen, watched her brother from the sofa as he checked the door locks again at midnight. "Bhaiya, sit," she said. "I'm fine," he said, and went to fill the water bottles. In the kitchen he stood holding the steel tumbler his father always used, and his throat closed. He put it down slowly. When Damini came in, he did not turn around quickly enough. She said nothing, just took the bottles from him. The next morning he asked his uncle to handle the visit to the electricity office, and let Damini book their mother's check-up.

qa.q: Where was Tanvir standing when his throat closed?
qa.a: He was standing in the kitchen, holding the steel tumbler his father always used.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he put the tumbler down, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was grieving. His throat closed, he set the tumbler down slowly, and he could not turn around quickly enough when Damini walked in.

qa.q: What small step showed Tanvir sharing the load instead of carrying it alone?
qa.a: He asked his uncle to handle the electricity office visit and let Damini book their mother's check-up, so the tasks were no longer all on him. 🤍

qa.q: How might Damini see her brother's constant checking and fixing?
qa.a: She may worry that he is hiding his own grief behind chores, which would explain why she tells him to sit and quietly takes the bottles from him.

grounding: An older sibling becomes the family's strong one after a death, cares for mother and sister, cracks privately, and starts sharing tasks.

passage: A month after the auto-rickshaw he was riding in skidded into a divider, Irfan still woke at 3 a.m. with his heart racing. Every horn on the road outside made his shoulders jump. He kept his morning routine anyway: tea, a short walk, the office bus at 8:40. At lunch his colleague Pooja noticed he had barely touched his rice. "You keep flinching," she said quietly. "It's been weeks. I should be over it," Irfan muttered. "I didn't tell the driver to slow down. Maybe if I had..." Pooja shook her head. "You were a passenger." She pulled up the number of the hospital's counselling desk on her phone. He looked at it for a long moment, then typed it into his own.

qa.q: How long after the crash did Irfan still wake at 3 a.m. with his heart racing?
qa.a: A month after the auto-rickshaw skidded into a divider, he still woke at 3 a.m. with his heart racing.

qa.q: Why does Irfan say he should be over it?
qa.a: He seems to think he is failing at recovering and blames himself, wondering whether telling the driver to slow down might have changed things.

qa.q: What would you advise Irfan to do next?
qa.a: Keep his daily routine going and actually call the hospital's counselling desk, since trained help suits a body that stays on alert after a scare.

qa.q: How does Pooja see Irfan's situation?
qa.a: She sees a colleague who is flinching and not eating, and who is not to blame because he was only a passenger, so she offers a concrete way to get help.

grounding: After a frightening accident the body stays alert and sleep is disturbed; Irfan keeps routines, is told it was not his fault, and takes down a counselling number.

passage: Avni pulled the shutter of her father's stationery shop halfway down and sat on the stool behind the counter without opening the ledger. It was ten months since the night the bus overturned near the canal bridge, and she still went quiet whenever anyone mentioned it. She had been the one who asked her cousin to take that late bus. Everyone said she should have moved on by now, so she said nothing, and the silence grew heavier. Jomon, who ran the tea stall next door, brought a glass of chai without being asked. "You've been sitting like that since morning." Avni's eyes filled. "It was my idea," she said. Jomon waited, then said, "There's a counsellor at the health centre on Thursdays. Want me to come along?" Avni nodded.

qa.q: Who brought Avni a glass of chai?
qa.a: Jomon, who ran the tea stall next door, brought a glass of chai without being asked.

qa.q: Why does Avni go quiet whenever anyone mentions the night of the bus accident?
qa.a: She blames herself because it was her idea for her cousin to take that late bus, and she feels others expect her to have moved on already.

qa.q: What could Avni and Jomon do next?
qa.a: Go to the counsellor at the health centre on Thursday, where Avni can say aloud what she has been carrying instead of sitting alone with it.

qa.q: What might Jomon have noticed about Avni that morning?
qa.a: Jomon saw Avni sitting motionless with the ledger unopened, which is likely why the chai arrived unasked and the offer to come along followed.

grounding: Avni blames herself for what happened and for still struggling; a trusted person offers a counsellor, and shame begins to be shared.

passage: Mahima, beta, you asked why Deepak Mama never says "forget it"? Sit, I'll tell you. When I was twenty-four, a truck hit my scooter near the flyover, and the friend riding behind me was badly hurt. For months I couldn't sleep, and I took the long road to work just to avoid that flyover. My father's cousins came to see me. One waved his hand and said, "Forget it, it's over. What will people say if you keep talking about it?" I nodded and went silent, as if a door had shut on me. Then my college friend Suresh sat with me at the tea shop and said, "Tell me only what you want to." I told him a little at a time. That was when I could breathe again.

qa.q: What did one of Deepak's father's cousins say when he waved his hand?
qa.a: He said, "Forget it, it's over. What will people say if you keep talking about it?"

qa.q: How did Deepak feel after being told to forget it, and what in the passage shows it?
qa.a: He felt silenced and shut out. He nodded and went quiet, as if a door had shut on him.

qa.q: What could a young person do who is told to forget a frightening event?
qa.a: Look for someone who believes them, as Deepak found in Suresh, and share only as much as they want, a little at a time.

qa.q: Why might the relative have said those words?
qa.a: Possibly out of worry about gossip and a wish to spare Deepak pain, though the effect was silencing, which shows that meaning and impact can differ.

grounding: Relatives dismiss the trauma with forget it and what will people say; Deepak recalls feeling silenced and being helped by a friend who let him share only what he wanted.

passage:
Tuesday, after the film: Jatin stopped walking outside the metro station. "Something happened to me at my old job. I've never told anyone." Amandeep's stomach dropped, but she kept her voice low. "I believe you. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to." They sat on the steps until his hands stopped shaking.

Saturday: Amandeep texted, "No need to reply. I'm around." He answered that evening with a single "thanks". She did not ask for details.

Two weeks later: Jatin asked whether she knew any counsellors. Amandeep found two clinic numbers and sent them with a question: "Want me to come with you, or would you rather go alone?" "Alone first," he said. She told nobody, not even her sister.

qa.q: What did Amandeep text on Saturday?
qa.a: She texted, "No need to reply. I'm around."

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling and wanting when Jatin told her?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped, so she was shaken, but she wanted Jatin to feel believed and unpressured, which is why she kept her voice low and said he need not tell her more.

qa.q: Which choice by Amandeep helped Jatin most, and why?
qa.a: Sending the clinic numbers and asking whether he wanted company or to go alone helped, because it let him keep control of his own pace.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Jatin when Amandeep asked no questions?
qa.a: He probably felt safer and less exposed, which fits with him replying with a thanks that evening and later asking about counsellors. 🤍

grounding: A friend confides being harmed; Amandeep believes, does not press for details, respects the pace, helps find counsellors and keeps the story private.

passage: Vaibhav, you asked how it actually went, so here it is, no polish. The first counsellor I saw, I froze for four sessions and counted ceiling tiles. It wasn't her fault, it just wasn't a fit, so I found someone else. With the new counsellor I said nothing big for weeks. Then one day I said one sentence about that night, just one, hands shaking, and nothing bad happened. The next week I said two. Some weeks I go backwards and can't say a word, and that's allowed. Remember when you texted, "Yamini, no pressure, tell me when you want"? I read that four times. My mum keeps asking when I'll be "better". I told her it's not one big moment. It's small safe things, again and again.

qa.q: For how many sessions did the speaker freeze and count ceiling tiles with the first counsellor?
qa.a: Four sessions, as the passage says, with the first counsellor.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel about the first counsellor, and why did Yamini switch?
qa.a: Yamini did not blame the counsellor but felt it was not a fit, so Yamini found someone else instead of forcing it.

qa.q: What does Yamini's account suggest about how trust grows in therapy?
qa.a: It grows through small safe steps, one sentence and then two, and some weeks go backwards, so patience matters more than one breakthrough.

qa.q: How might Yamini's mother be seeing the recovery?
qa.a: She seems to expect a moment when Yamini will be better, so she may not notice how much the small steps count until it is explained to her.

grounding: Yamini slowly begins to trust a counsellor, tries another when the first is a poor fit, and describes healing as small repeated acts of safety.

passage:
March 4: Chaitanya had filed a complaint with HR about her manager's repeated unwelcome remarks six weeks earlier. Today the email said "no action warranted", and her project was moved to another team. She read it twice, hot with anger, and felt small.

March 6: She told her old colleague Lalit over the phone. "They punished you for reporting," he said. "That isn't on you." He asked if she had saved her emails. She had, in a folder called "Misc".

March 20: She sat in a legal aid clinic with printouts, dates in order, while Lalit waited outside with two cups of tea. The volunteer explained she could also take the matter to the company's internal committee. Chaitanya wrote the first line of the letter right there.

qa.q: In which folder had Chaitanya saved her emails?
qa.a: She had saved them in a folder called "Misc".

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel after reading the HR email?
qa.a: She felt angry and small, reading it twice, 'hot with anger'.

qa.q: Which steps helped Chaitanya move forward?
qa.a: Keeping her emails, putting the dates in order, telling Lalit, and going to a legal aid clinic to learn about the internal committee gave her a way forward.

qa.q: How does Lalit see what happened to Chaitanya?
qa.a: He sees it as punishment for reporting and not something she did wrong, which is why he tells her it isn't on her and waits outside with tea.

grounding: A workplace ignored and effectively punished a complaint; Chaitanya keeps records, is believed by a friend and turns to legal aid and the internal committee.

passage: Thomas had eleven minutes before his counsellor's appointment, and the auto was stuck behind a wedding procession. His phone buzzed: a reply from the hostel warden, three lines, nothing about the seniors who had hurt him two years ago or the complaints he had made. His thumb hovered over the screen. He typed, I hope you lose your job, then held down delete. Beside him sat Chinmay, a friend from the hostel, who said, "Say what you actually want." Thomas breathed out. "I want them to admit it. I want the college to have a proper committee." He drafted a short email asking for a written response and a meeting with the principal, and saved it for the counsellor to read before sending. The procession finally moved.

qa.q: How many minutes did Thomas have before his counsellor's appointment?
qa.a: He had eleven minutes.

qa.q: What did Thomas really want when he deleted his angry line?
qa.a: He wanted the harm to be admitted and the college to set up a proper committee, not revenge on the warden, so he deleted the angry line.

qa.q: How did Thomas turn his anger into something useful?
qa.a: He drafted a short email asking for a written response and a meeting with the principal, and saved it for the counsellor to read before sending.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see Thomas's first typed message?
qa.a: Chinmay probably understands the fury but nudges Thomas with "Say what you actually want", hinting that the angry line would not bring Thomas what he needs.

grounding: Thomas's anger at those who harmed him and failed to protect him is channelled into a written request and a meeting through proper channels instead of revenge, despite time pressure.

passage:
Dear Dilnaz,

Guess what: I slept straight through until six on Wednesday, and no dreams I remember. I lay there almost suspicious. Then on Friday I laughed properly at Ammi's joke about the neighbour's parrot, and afterwards I felt a pinch of guilt, as if I had stolen something. I told my counsellor, and she said joy is not a betrayal of what happened. I'm trying to believe her. Last weekend I even went to the market by myself and picked out a yellow scarf. Remember when I couldn't be in crowds? It hasn't vanished, but it doesn't run my day. Thank you for never rushing me. Come over on Sunday, Ammi is making biryani, and I'd like to celebrate a little.

Love,
Zeenat

qa.q: What colour scarf did Zeenat pick out at the market?
qa.a: Zeenat picked out a yellow scarf.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat feel a pinch of guilt after laughing at the parrot joke?
qa.a: Zeenat felt as if joy was something stolen, as though laughing meant betraying what happened.

qa.q: How could Zeenat and Dilnaz celebrate the progress?
qa.a: Dilnaz could come over on Sunday for biryani with Ammi, marking the good days without any pressure. 🎉

qa.q: What might Dilnaz feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably relief and gladness, and perhaps warmth at being thanked for never rushing Zeenat, since the letter credits that patience directly.

grounding: Small good days return; Zeenat lets joy in despite guilt, celebrates better sleep and trusting a friend, and notes the past no longer rules the day.

passage: I've sat next to Devika for three years, so I noticed when she stopped celebrating. She got the senior analyst title in March, the one she'd wanted since college, and by April she was staring at the ceiling fan during lunch. One evening she said, "Manjula, I got everything on my list. Why do I feel like nothing?" I honestly didn't know what to say. Maybe she's just tired, or maybe it's bigger. Then she started staying back on Thursdays to teach two interns spreadsheets, and she came in looking lighter. She also phoned her old school teacher. I can't say what's going on in her head, but she seems to be looking for something other than titles.

qa.q: What title did Devika get in March?
qa.a: She got the senior analyst title in March.

qa.q: What was Devika wondering when she asked why she felt like nothing?
qa.a: She was wondering what it was all for, since she had ticked off everything on her list and still felt empty.

qa.q: What small commitments could help Devika find meaning?
qa.a: Keeping up things like teaching the interns and staying in touch with her old school teacher, small ongoing commitments to people and craft.

qa.q: How sure can Manjula be about Devika's inner state?
qa.a: Not sure at all. Manjula says it might be tiredness or something bigger, and only reports what was seen, such as the teaching and the phone call.

grounding: After reaching early goals Devika asks what it was all for; a coworker observes her turning toward teaching and relationships rather than status.
